name: Semmelweis reflex
statement: The reflex-like rejection of new evidence because it contradicts an established belief, named for the Vienna obstetrician whose handwashing results his colleagues dismissed.
meaning: The name asserts a mechanism rather than an outcome. It says the evidence is refused because of the conflict, before it is weighed, and Robert Anton Wilson's original definition went further and had the group punish the discoverer. Testing that would mean showing the same evidence judged worse when it cuts against a held position, and judged that way without engagement. Three separate things travel under the name and pull apart on inspection: a real episode in Vienna between 1846 and 1861, a retelling of it that has the numbers and the reception wrong, and a phrase coined in 1979 that never became a research programme.

origin.where: The Game of Life, by Timothy Leary
origin.note: The definition sits in a footnote on page 43 and is presented as an entry from a fictional reference work, 'Webster's Galactic Dictionary, 23rd Edition': 'Mob behavior found among primates and larval hominids on undeveloped planets, in which a discovery of important scientific fact is punished rather than rewarded.' The book is a treatment of the Tarot as a map of evolution. Its title page credits Leary as author and Wilson with its historical and scholarly scripts. The copy read for this entry is the 1993 New Falcon printing, copyright 1979.

evidence: Semmelweis was appointed in 1846 to the Vienna Maternity Hospital, which ran two clinics. The first taught doctors and medical students, the second trained midwives, and women were admitted on alternate days with no clinical selection. Loudon calls that a controlled trial by accident rather than design. From 1840 through 1846 the two clinics recorded 42,795 births and 2,977 maternal deaths. Mortality ran at 98.4 per 1,000 births in the first clinic against 36.2 per 1,000 in the second. In May 1847 Semmelweis required students to wash in chloride of lime before entering the first clinic. In 1848 the first clinic recorded 12.7 maternal deaths per 1,000 births, against 13.3 in the second. Loudon read those figures from Table XXIV of Semmelweis's own treatise. La Rochelle and Julien used the monthly series instead. Average monthly mortality was 10.65% from January 1841 to May 1847 and 1.98% from the introduction of handwashing to February 1849, a risk ratio of 5.38. Their interrupted time-series model put the handwashing coefficient at 0.0887 with a standard error of 0.0310, p = 0.0042, which they describe as an absolute reduction of 8.87% and as one death avoided for every eleven women examined. Semmelweis held that childbed fever was caused by decaying animal-organic matter absorbed through the placental bed or through injuries sustained in delivery. Bacteria had no part in it. Pasteur's work was still a decade off.

replication.headline: No study measuring the Semmelweis reflex as named was found; the two nearest measured things are an 8.6% rise in outside publications after an eminent scientist dies, and 2,034 citations to papers that had already been retracted.
replication.detail: Azoulay, Fons-Rosen and Graff Zivin tracked entry into the subfields of 452 star life scientists who died while still active. Publications by the star's previous collaborators fell 20.7%. Publications by non-collaborators rose 8.6%, the rise came in the highly cited articles, and the growth was carried by papers that do not cite the star at all. The authors then rule out the reading the title invites. In the five years before death only three of the 452 sat on NIH study sections and only three were journal editors, so the stars were not blocking anything. What the paper measures is deterrence, outsiders staying away while a luminary is alive, which is not the refusal of evidence the reflex describes. These figures were read from NBER working paper 21788, the authors' own preprint, not from the published article. The other measured neighbour runs in the opposite direction. Budd, Sievert and Schultz identified 235 articles retracted between 1966 and 1997 and counted 2,034 citations to them after the retraction notice. Of 299 citations examined, 19 noted the retraction and 280 treated the article as valid, 17 explicitly and 263 by implication. That is discredited work surviving, rather than sound work being refused.

limits: The reflex has never been operationalised. A Europe PMC search for the phrase returned 32 records, the earliest from 2009, and every one is an editorial, a historical piece, a narrative review or a commentary using the phrase as an ornament. A Crossref search returned book chapters and opinion articles with the same character. Gupta and colleagues' review in World Neurosurgery is typical: it searched the term, retold the Vienna story and offered advice, and measured nothing. Searches covered Europe PMC, Crossref, the DataCite and Crossref DOI records for every citation here, Google Books, the Internet Archive and the open web. The historical record is itself contested. Tulodziecki argues that Semmelweis was a careless reasoner and that the puzzle of his rejection dissolves once that is admitted. Kadar and Croft answer that her account of his theory has no basis in fact and rests on a misreading of the sequence of events in 1847. Loudon, who is hostile to the hagiography, still calls the observations original and astute, and separately notes that Semmelweis was intolerant of criticism to the point of paranoia and that his treatise mixes clarity with muddled and bellicose attacks on his critics. Nothing in the sources read here settles which account of the rejection is right.
misreadings: The famous figures are wrong. The fall from about 18% to about 2% comes from Hebra's editorial of December 1847, which set two unrepresentative averages beside each other. April and May 1847 gave 17.2%, or 96 deaths in 558 women, and were taken to stand for the period before handwashing, although January, February and March of the same year had run at 3.21%, 1.02% and 3.6%. The rates Loudon takes from the treatise are 98.4 and 36.2 deaths per 1,000 births for the two clinics, and Wieger's annual rate for the first clinic in 1848 was 1.27%, from 45 deaths against a previous range of 238 to 521 a year. The improvement also did not hold at the 1848 level. Across 1848 to 1859 the first clinic ran at 35.7 deaths per 1,000 births and the second at 30.6. The silence is a myth too. Hebra announced the discovery in print in December 1847 and asked other institutions for confirming or disconfirming results, Wieger published the actual figures in the Gazette médicale de Strasbourg on 20 April 1849, Skoda described the work to the Imperial Academy of Sciences on 18 October 1849, and Semmelweis gave his own first public account to the Society of Physicians on 15 May 1850. His treatise, dated 1861, appeared in 1860, thirteen years after the intervention. What the record shows is not refusal to look but a specific objection to the inference. The Gazette médicale de Paris granted the fall in 1850 and denied that it followed from the washing, since epidemics of puerperal fever were known to fluctuate and the rate might have dropped for another reason. Kadar and Croft argue from Lesky's archive documents that Semmelweis's chief, Johann Klein, refused the evidence on that same ground, and that Semmelweis ran his rabbit experiments to answer it. Post hoc is not propter hoc, and the men who said so were right about the logic even though they were wrong about the world. Antisepsis reached obstetrics in the 1880s through Lister, who had not heard of Semmelweis until his own method was established. Wilson's glossary entry, finally, describes puerperal fever as a now-obsolete disease.

Tulodziecki, D. (2013). Shattering the myth of Semmelweis. Philosophy of Science, 80(5), 1065-1075. Read from its abstract and from Kadar and Croft's account of it; the full text was not obtained.

Leary, T. (1979/1993). The Game of Life. Phoenix: New Falcon Publications, p. 43. Historical and scholarly scripts by Robert Anton Wilson. The source of the phrase; read in the Internet Archive scan of the 1993 printing.
